answer.rationale: Rollback is excluded outright by compliance (security patch must not be reverted), so memory_b1 is not actionable regardless of its content. The observed pattern—climbing write-path p99 during peak settlement load—matches the capacity-constraint scenario in memory_b3 (headroom provisioning kept queue depth flat during a peak surge) more closely than a dependency failure (memory_b4) or a regional degradation (memory_b2). I verified memory_b3 to confirm the original record supports add_capacity as low-risk to in-flight writes, and pulled memory_b4 to rule out that this is instead a dependency-failure pattern better suited to circuit breaking, since misdiagnosing a write-latency spike as pure capacity shortfall when it's actually a downstream dependency problem would waste the single intervention window. Regional failover and read-replica routing were deprioritized: failover carries real risk of dropping in-flight writes during a failover cutover, which conflicts with the 'without losing customer writes' objective, and read-replica routing only offloads reads, not the write path that's actually degraded. Given this is happening at daily peak with real settlement money at stake, I'm sizing the capacity addition as a standard, monitored rollout rather than a full broad rollout, since I can't fully rule out that the release itself (not just load) is contributing to latency, and want to observe effect before committing further headroom.
